topics.topic: Audit-log erasure records must represent the cutoff date without a customer or project reference
questions: What does the governance record store for an audit-entry erasure, which touches neither a customer nor a project and requires the cutoff date rather than a `customer_ref` or `project_id`?
How does this record represent an audit-log erasure, which touches neither a customer nor a project, and where does it store the cutoff date needed to repeat `erase audit entries before a date`?

judgement.why: This is the same audit-erasure subject and cutoff-date question decided in P3, and its deciding passages have not changed.

precedent.topic: Representation and cutoff-date field for audit-entry erasure without a customer or project identifier
quotes:
the subject, by identity only (R0-37), one of a closed set fixed by the
  action (owner, 2026-10-31; codex round-02 T4): the project (`project_id`)
  for a project's actions; the customer (`customer_ref`) for a customer's
  actions, restricting and lifting, ending and resuming; the session and the
  project for a grant or a revocation; for the import, the digest of the file
  it accepted (M10) — the migration closure is unique in the instance and has
  no other identity (codex round-04 T1); none for an erasure of old entries,
  whose fact is the owner's date;
for an erasure of old entries: the date the owner gave (R0-66).
precedent.why: State 1 specifies that an audit-entry erasure has no entity subject and stores the owner-provided cutoff date as its own fact.

topics.topic: Import replay record must preserve source mappings and minted customer identities
questions: What exact durable record links every picked source project to the display name and optional alias needed to repeat the same import?

What preserves the `customer_ref` values minted during the lost import for legacy customers, so a repeated import either recreates the same identities or explicitly repairs consumers that observed the first identities?

quotes:
A store lost before a checked backup holds the import
loses the import with it, and the import may then be made again: the owner
keeps the export file and the picks, names and aliases given in the import
until a checked backup holds the import, and retires the VPS instance only
then (R0-79).
Customer's `customer_ref` is minted when the import is accepted.

A store lost before a checked backup holds the import loses it,
   and the import may then be made again (R0-89).
judgement.divergence: One implementation preserves and reuses the customer identities minted by the lost import; another mints different `customer_ref` values on the repeated import and requires affected consumer references to be repaired, which the owner and consumer services notice.
judgement.why: The retained choices cover projects, names and aliases but do not preserve or deterministically reconstruct the customer identities minted by the lost import.

topics.topic: Migration vault must be identified and governed as a temporary personal-data storage boundary
questions: Does “the vault” mean the named Bitwarden system, and if so who hosts and can access the export and import choices containing personal data?

Are the retained export and import choices an explicit temporary exception to R0-80's rule that Registry and its stated exceptions are the only homes of personal data, and exactly when does that exception begin and end?

Does the Bitwarden vault become a governed recipient and storage boundary for migration personal data, including its own replicas, history and deletion behavior, or does "vault" name a different owner-controlled store?

quotes:
The owner generates each service token and the staff credential, keeps the
original in the owner's own password vault (Bitwarden), and writes it into
Registry's configuration and into the configuration of its holders: a service
token into the one service it names, the one staff credential into each tool
acting as staff — the operator, a frontend server.
Neither Registry nor any holder reaches the vault; the platform has no secret manager.

The kept export and the import's choices hold
personal data: the owner keeps them in the vault (R0-23), the governance
lists them as a copy that remains, as R0-81 lists the services' copies, and
the owner deletes them once a checked backup holds the import.
judgement.divergence: One implementation stores the migration material in a provider-hosted Bitwarden vault with provider-managed replicas and history; another stores it in an owner-hosted vault wholly inside the owner's boundary, which changes who receives or retains the personal data and is noticed by the owner, the governance record and the vault service.
judgement.why: The text identifies Bitwarden and the logical deletion point but does not name its host, other principals with access, or whether provider replicas and history are inside the temporary personal-data boundary.

topics.topic: Recovery must define correction actions, completion evidence, and unreconstructable-fact failures
questions: What concrete action constitutes “corrects it,” what evidence may the owner use when one of those records is missing, and what observable result marks the correction complete?

What concrete action constitutes correcting the store when the retention record or export is missing, what observable result marks completion, and what failure is reported when the lost facts cannot be reconstructed?

quotes:
Where the
retention record or the kept export is missing, what the restored store holds stands until the owner
corrects it.

The owner first starts the restored instance owner-only (A17 rule 1), so
   no service and no agent reaches it, and brings each Customer and project to
   the state the owner's own record of the retention review (R0-60) gives for
   it now — erased, restricted, ended or not — and erases audit entries before
   the latest date the owner erased by, before configuring the tokens and
   starting it again.

This is the owner's operation (Explicit exclusions: the
   host's administration), and the owner's record is its evidence; Registry,
   which no longer holds those changes, cannot list them, enforce them or
   tell when this is done. Its guarantee after a restore is what the backup
   held.
judgement.divergence: One implementation leaves the instance owner-only until the owner reconstructs every missing fact through ordinary actions and explicitly restarts it; another permits service access with unreconstructable facts left as the backup held or supplies a recovery-specific correction failure, which the owner, agents and services notice through availability and record state.
judgement.why: The text defines recovery when the owner's records exist but hides the missing-record case behind “corrects it” without naming an action, observable completion or failure when reconstruction is impossible.

topics.topic: Retention replay must define covered transitions and deterministic action ordering
questions: Does the record and replay obligation also cover inverse actions such as lifting a restriction and resuming a relationship, and does an erasure kind distinguish customer erasure, project anonymisation and project deletion?
How are multiple recorded actions ordered when they have the same date or when later actions reverse earlier ones?

Does the recovery record and replay include inverse transitions such as lifting a restriction and resuming a relationship, and are transitions replayed chronologically or reduced to the latest resulting state?

judgement.why: This is the same question about inverse transitions, erasure variants and chronological replay versus restoration to current recorded state decided in P1, and its deciding passages have not changed.

precedent.topic: Complete scope of retention actions and transitions that must be replayed
quotes:
The owner first starts the restored instance owner-only (A17 rule 1), so
   no service and no agent reaches it, and brings each Customer and project to
   the state the owner's own record of the retention review (R0-60) gives for
   it now — erased, restricted, ended or not — and erases audit entries before
   the latest date the owner erased by, before configuring the tokens and
   starting it again.
precedent.why: State 2 requires restoration to the current recorded state rather than replaying every historical transition, so lifted restrictions, resumed relationships and the current erased or unerased state are covered by the final state the record gives.

topics.topic: Handling consumer-visible effects when an import is rolled back and repeated
questions: Can Registry and its consumers use the imported records before a checked backup holds them, and if so, what happens to consumer-side effects created from the first import when Registry rolls back and repeats it?

topics.topic: Relationship-end replay must distinguish action date from effective end date
questions: For an end-of-relationship action, is “its date” the date the action was performed or the possibly earlier effective end date that must be supplied when repeating it, and must both be recorded?

topics.topic: Scope of Registry guarantees after restoring an older backup
questions: Does history-local validity narrow only audit numbering and import closure, as R0-89's heading says, or every Registry guarantee, including erasure, restriction and ended-relationship guarantees that an older backup can reverse?

topics.topic: Stable identifier distinguishing separate store histories
questions: What identifies one store history from another so duplicate audit numbering and repeated import closure can be distinguished in audit output and governance records?

topics.topic: Whether a restored Registry may operate before replay and correction complete
questions: May the restored Registry serve normal reads and billing data while erased data, restrictions or relationship endings are missing, despite R0-51, R0-65 and the erasure promises, or must it refuse affected disclosures until correction is complete?
